sentences.text: Grabauornis was an extinct genus of enantiornithean birds that lived in China during the Early Cretaceous.
The holotype — the specimen the species is based on — consists of a well-preserved skeleton that is compressed onto a single plate.
This bird possessed a unique sternum where the center extends further back than the fan-shaped side wings.
It had a relatively short head equipped with small, conical teeth.
Its hand featured robust second and third finger phalanges, a third metacarpal extending beyond the second, and a hand shorter than the ulna.
The shoulder blade was long, narrow, and tapered towards the top.
Grabauornis possessed an alula, a thumb feather that likely served as a nose vane, confirming its flying ability.
Researchers suggest that Grabauornis had a good ability to fly because its humerus-to-ulna ratio was below the 130% threshold required for ground-dwelling.
The species Grabauornis lingyuanensis was named and described in 2014 by Johan Dalsätt, Per Ericson, and Zhou Zhonghe.
The specific name lingyuanensis refers to the city of Lingyuan in the Liaoning province of China where the fossil was found.
The holotype fossil was found in the Yixian Formation, which dates to the Aptian age of 125 million years ago.
Grabauornis had a humerus length of 95% of its ulna, which is an average ratio compared to other enantiornitheans.
Grabauornis belongs to the parent group Euenantiornithes.
Grabauornis lived during the Barremian to Aptian stages, from 125.77 to 119.57 million years ago.
